title: The First Rule of Bible Study Is Context
subtitle: Why reading Bible verses in context matters, and how to interpret a verse within its paragraph, its book, and the whole canon of Scripture

sections.title: The One Rule Under All the Others
sections.body:
If a person learned only one principle of Bible study and obeyed it, they would already read better than most. The rule is context. A text without a context is a pretext for whatever you wanted to say.

We have built a whole culture of misreading on the verse, plucked clean from its surroundings and printed on a card. The chapter and verse numbers, added centuries after the books were written, have done us a quiet harm. They have trained us to see the Bible as a bin of detachable sentences instead of a library of arguments, stories, and songs that move from a beginning to an end.

No author wrote in verses. Paul wrote letters. Moses wrote books. David wrote whole poems. The meaning lives in the flow, and the moment you cut a sentence out of the flow, you are free to make it mean nearly anything. That freedom is the danger. Context is the cure.

sections.title: The Verse in Its Paragraph
sections.body:
Start with the smallest circle. Before a verse can mean anything, it has to mean something in the paragraph around it, in the immediate argument the author was making.

Read what comes before. Read what comes after. Ask what question the writer was answering when he wrote your favorite line. Philippians 4:13, the verse about doing all things through Christ, sits in a paragraph about contentment in plenty and in want, where Paul is saying he has learned to be at peace whether full or hungry. The verse is about endurance through scarcity, not a guarantee of victory in the playoffs. The paragraph tells you so, if you read it.

The joint words guide you here. A therefore, a but, a because: these are the author showing you how his thoughts connect. Follow them. The paragraph is the first place a verse is held accountable, and most misreadings die right there, the instant you read the sentence on either side.

sections.title: The Paragraph in Its Book
sections.body:
Widen the circle. Each paragraph belongs to a whole book that has its own purpose, its own situation, its own argument running from first page to last.

A book was written by one author to address something specific. Galatians burns with a fight over whether Gentiles must be circumcised to belong to Christ, and every paragraph in it serves that fight. James presses a community that had divorced its faith from its works. Read a paragraph as though it floated free of the book, and you will miss the pressure that gave it its shape and force.

So ask what this book is doing as a whole, and where your passage falls in its movement. Is this the problem being stated or the solution being delivered. Is this the indictment or the comfort that follows it. A paragraph read in light of the book's whole purpose says something far sharper and truer than the same paragraph read alone. The book is the second courtroom, and it overturns a lot of verdicts the paragraph let stand.

sections.title: The Book in the Whole of Scripture
sections.body:
The last circle is the largest. Every book sits inside one library, one story, one canon that runs from creation to new creation, and Scripture is finally its own best interpreter.

This is the old principle that the clear texts interpret the unclear ones, and that no single passage can be made to contradict the settled witness of the whole. When you meet a hard verse, you read it in the light of the brighter ones, not the other way around. A doctrine built on one obscure sentence, against the grain of the entire Bible, is a doctrine built on sand.

But hold this circle with care, because it can be abused too. The canon does not give you permission to flatten a passage into whatever your system prefers, drowning the particular voice of the text in a chorus of cross references. Let the verse speak in its paragraph and its book first. Then let the whole canon confirm and deepen it. From the paragraph, to the book, to the Bible entire. Read in all three circles, and the text will hold its own meaning against you, which is exactly what it should do.

sections.title: Context Is a Discipline of Submission
sections.body:
Reading in context is not mainly a technique. It is a posture. It is the decision to let the author finish his sentence before you decide what he meant.

That decision costs you something. It takes from you the freedom to make the Bible say what you came hoping it would say.

The verse ripped from its setting is a useful thing if your goal is to win an argument or comfort yourself cheaply. The verse left in its setting is harder to control, which is the whole reason we keep ripping it out. I have done it from a pulpit, fond of a sentence and unwilling to read the paragraph that would have ruined my point. Context is the discipline that catches that hand in the act. Read the whole thing. Let the text outvote you. You did not come to make the Bible agree with you. You came to find out where it does not, and to be changed there.
